Empirical Research Plan: Minimum-Wage Effects on Restaurant Earnings and Employment, 1990-2006  

-----------------------------------------------------------------------
1. Identification Strategy  
-----------------------------------------------------------------------
Primary strategy: Two-way fixed-effects Difference-in-Differences (DID) implemented within contiguous state-border county pairs, supplemented by an event-study specification.  

Why appropriate  
• Rich policy variation – 49 state or federal hikes generate many “natural experiments.”  
• Border counties are close substitutes in labor-productivity drivers (weather, industry mix, demographics) yet face different statutory minima, strengthening the parallel-trends claim.  
• County- and quarter-fixed effects absorb all time-invariant county factors and common macro shocks, while county-pair×quarter FEs sweep out spatially varying aggregate cycles (e.g., faster Southern growth).  
• An event study provides a visual and statistical pre-trend test and dynamic treatment profile.  

-----------------------------------------------------------------------
2. Treatment and Control  
-----------------------------------------------------------------------
Treatment variable  
MW_ct ≡ log(real statutory minimum wage) prevailing in county c, quarter t.  
Treated observation = a county-quarter in which MW_ct increased relative to its previously constant level.  

Control group  
The adjacent county across the state line in the same pair whose minimum wage did not change (or changed later). Because the regression uses within-pair contrasts, the untreated county-quarter provides the counterfactual.  

Treatment timing / event date  
Quarter in which a state (or federal) minimum-wage increase becomes effective. For the event study, define τ = 0 as the first quarter the new rate is binding. Leads τ ≤ −4 and lags τ ≥ 1 trace dynamics.  

Running variable / cutoff  
Not needed—this is a DID, not RDD. (The spatial discontinuity is incorporated through county-pair fixed effects rather than a running variable.)  

-----------------------------------------------------------------------
3. Key Identifying Assumptions  
-----------------------------------------------------------------------
A1. Parallel trends within pairs. Absent a MW change, employment/earnings in the two border counties would follow the same path.  
→ Plausibility: Border counties share labor markets; pair-specific pre-trend tests can be performed.  

A2. No spillovers across the state border large enough to offset treatment.  
→ Plausibility: Some commuting exists, but restaurants are local-services firms with limited cross-border relocation ability. We can down-weight high-commuting pairs.  

A3. Policy exogeneity at the county-pair level. State legislators do not time MW hikes in direct response to restaurant employment in a single border county.  
→ Plausibility: State laws are crafted for broader constituencies; restaurant employment is <10 % of the non-farm workforce.  

A4. Stable composition. MW hikes do not systematically change county boundaries or NAICS definitions.  
→ Plausibility: QCEW coding stable; verify with line-of-business codes.  

-----------------------------------------------------------------------
4. Major Threats and Mitigations  
-----------------------------------------------------------------------
T1. Differential pre-trends (violate A1).  
• Mitigation: Event-study plots; drop/cluster pairs with significant pre-trends; allow county-specific linear trends.  

T2. Cross-border spillovers (violate A2).  
• Mitigation: Exclude metro areas with >30 % cross-state commuting; test for spillovers on accommodation, retail, manufacturing.  

T3. Heterogeneous treatment timing bias in TWFE DID.  
• Mitigation: Use interaction-weighted estimator à la Sun & Abraham (2021) or Callaway & Sant’Anna (2020) rather than classic TWFE; results robust to both.  

-----------------------------------------------------------------------
5. R Code Outline (executable)  
-----------------------------------------------------------------------
```r
# 0. Packages ----------------------------------------------------------
library(data.table)
library(fixest)        # fast high-dimensional FE & Sun-Abraham
library(lubridate)
library(ggplot2)

# 1. Load data ---------------------------------------------------------
# Assume three CSVs: county_qcew.csv, minw_state_qtr.csv, border_pairs.csv
qcew   <- fread("county_qcew.csv")          # emp & earnings by county-qtr
minw   <- fread("minw_state_qtr.csv")       # nominal MW by state-qtr
pairs  <- fread("border_pairs.csv")         # county_id, pair_id

# 2. Merge & construct variables --------------------------------------
setkey(qcew, state, county, year, quarter)
setkey(minw, state, year, quarter)
dt <- merge(qcew, minw, by = c("state","year","quarter"))
dt <- merge(dt, pairs, by = c("state","county"))

# Real MW (deflate by CPI that equals 100 in 2000)
dt[, lnmw := log(min_wage / cpi)]

# Outcomes
dt[, ln_emp     := log(total_emp) ]            # employment
dt[, ln_payroll := log(avg_weekly_earn) ]      # earnings

# Event-study relative time
dt[, eff_qtr := ifelse(lnmw != shift(lnmw, 1, type="lag"), quarter, NA),
   by = state]                                 # first qtr of change
dt[, g := min(eff_qtr, na.rm=TRUE), by = state] # group (first treat yr-qtr)
dt[, relt := (year*4 + quarter) - g ]           # leads/lags

# 3. Main DID within border pairs -------------------------------------
main_mod <- feols(ln_emp ~ lnmw | pair_id + quarter, 
                  cluster = ~state, data = dt)
etable(main_mod)

# 4. Sun-Abraham event study ------------------------------------------
es_mod <- feols(ln_emp ~ sunab(g, relt) | pair_id + quarter, 
                cluster = ~state, data = dt[!is.infinite(relt)])
iplot(es_mod, ref.line = 0)

# 5. Robustness: add county-specific trends ---------------------------
main_trend <- feols(ln_emp ~ lnmw | pair_id + quarter + county, 
                    cluster = ~state,
                    data = dt[, year_ctr := year - 1990][, .(ln_emp, lnmw,
                               pair_id, quarter, county, state, year_ctr)],
                    add_fes = ~ county^year_ctr)   # interacted FE for trends
etable(main_mod, main_trend)
```

-----------------------------------------------------------------------
6. Expected Results  
-----------------------------------------------------------------------
Earnings: Positive and sizable. A 10 % MW increase should raise average restaurant weekly earnings by ~1.5–2.5 %.  

Employment: Theory with monopsony and frictions predicts small to zero elasticities. Prior suggests −0.02 to +0.01 (i.e., a 10 % MW hike changes restaurant employment by −0.2 % to +0.1 %). Hence we expect statistically insignificant employment effects concentrated near zero.  

-----------------------------------------------------------------------
7. Validity Checklist Self-Assessment (DID)  
-----------------------------------------------------------------------
C1. Pre-trend equivalence visually confirmed ……............... 1  
C2. No simultaneous confounders within county pairs .......... 0.5  
C3. No interference/spillovers across units .................. 0.5  
C4. Correct functional form & treatment measurement .......... 1  
C5. Robustness to alternative estimators (SA, CS) ............ 1  

Total score: 4/5 – credible but not bulletproof; spillovers and confounders remain the main caveats.
